verdicts.why: Names an unpleasant feeling in a plain, slightly formal word; the dread is the referent, and the word takes no side on the person feeling it.
A neutral legal term for an arrest; it describes the act without approving or disapproving of it.
The word names a hostile emotion but does not itself judge; one can report that someone felt contempt, or deserved it, with no attitude of the speaker's attached - a bad referent, not a loaded word.
Open disrespect is the meaning, and the strength of that meaning is not an attitude beyond it; the plain word for the thing.
Means to declare with authority or formality; the formality is register, not a judgement of what is declared, and the irony in Austen's uses comes from her context rather than the verb.
To articulate or utter in a certain way is a plain description of speech with no attitude attached.
A formal-register synonym of help; choosing it over help says something about register, not about the speaker's view of the helper or the helped.
Describes a subordinate supporting role factually; the subordination is the meaning, not a slight.
To work for or serve someone is stated plainly here, with no contempt or deference built into the word.
Describes the manner of an utterance (sudden, emotional) without judging the speaker or what was said.
In the state-or-announce sense it is a plain reporting verb with no attitude.
Uninterrupted in time is a factual description; the sentences show it applied equally to welcome things (society, practice) and unwelcome ones (vexation), so the word carries no side.
Unvarying in nature is a neutral property; nothing in the word approves or dismisses what it describes.
A formal synonym of have for attributes and skills; the register is elevated but no attitude toward the possessor or the trait is added.
Ownership stated in a formal word; it describes without judging.
An emotion or idea taking control is the meaning of this sense; the loss of agency it describes is a strong meaning, not a judgement laid on top of it.
Names the comfort felt when consoled; a pleasant referent named plainly, with no attitude of the speaker in the word.
The act of giving relief in affliction, stated neutrally; the word does not praise or belittle the consoler.
A short personal letter, named plainly; no attitude toward the writer, the recipient, or the contents.
A brief written record is a purely descriptive label.
A technical term of music notation with no evaluative content.
A concrete name for a type of carriage; the disdain in 'hack chaise' comes from hack, not from chaise.
A piece of furniture named plainly; nothing in the word judges it.
A neutral name for a musical instrument (here the pianoforte); it describes and does not judge.
A device requiring skill is a functional, descriptive category with no attitude attached.
